newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Poison extortion threat hits east coast Australia.
newsitem.headline: Poison extortion threat hits east coast Australia.

text.p: Australia's largest biscuit manufacturer on Friday ordered all its products removed from supermarkets along Australia's east coast after an extortionist threatened to plant poisoned biscuits in stores from Monday.

The extortionist has demanded police involved in a 1991 murder case take a lie detector test in an attempt to prove the innocence of a friend now serving a life sentence for the execution-style murder of a bookmaker.
"I think this is the worst nightmare of every food manufacturer in the world," said Queensland detective superintendent Ron Pickering.

"We are doing everything possible to minimise the threat and guarantee the safety of consumers. We ask that people remain vigilant and exercise common sense in their shopping habits," Pickering told a news conference.

The extortionist laced Monte Carlo cream biscuits made by Arnotts with a pesticide and sent packages of the poisoned biscuits, along with an letter, to Arnotts, politicians and a media organisation in the states of New South Wales and Queensland on February 3, police said.
"It's a poison that can kill people...but other poisons can kill you quicker," New South Wales detective chief superintendent Clive Small told a Sydney news conference.
The letter demanded that New South Wales police involved in the murder investigation of bookmaker Peter Wade and his girlfriend in 1991 take a polygraph test by February 17.

The letter claimed Ronald Thomas, 46, who is serving a life sentence for the shooting murders, is innocent and that the real killers remain free. "This is not a one-off event, it will be a campaign of attacks until this is resolved," the letter said.
Police have rejected the extortionist's demand. "We are not prepared to entertain these types of threats or demands," Pickering said.
Police have said an arrest warrant exists for John Bobak, who is wanted for the 1991 murder, but would not say whether he was a suspect in the extortion.

Police said Arnotts was not the target of the extortionist, but merely the vehicle chosen to put pressure on state governments. They said they feared other food companies may become involved in the extortion.
Arnotts, about 70 percent owned by U.S. food processing giant Campbell Soup Co, has had trading in its shares halted pending an announcement by the company.
"I stress that Arnotts is an innocent victim in this threat," Pickering said.
"It is not only Arnotts that we would be concerned about," he said, adding the poisoned biscuits were not laced in the production process, but after being bought by the extortionist.

Queensland health department spokesman Dr John Scott said the laced biscuits had been carefully taken apart and the unnamed pesticide mixed with a vegetable dye and the cream filling and then reassembled.

Scott said the laced biscuits had a slight discolouration as a result of the vegetable dye and an odour. "While people should look for colouring or an odour, we can't assume that will continue," he said.
Arnotts said it had decided to recall all its products from Australia's east coast states of New South Wales and Queensland on Friday.
"That decision was not taken lightly and by God I wish I did not have to take it," said Chris Roberts, Arnotts's chief executive officer.
However, Roberts said he believed all Arnotts products on supermarket shelves and now in homes were safe.
"On all the evidence there will be no threat to products until the 17th of this month, which is next Monday," he said.
